questions.explanation:
Right ventricular pressure during systole (about 25 mmHg) is far below aortic pressure, so the RV wall does not squeeze its vessels shut and right coronary flow continues in systole.
Not A: right-dominant circulation is the most common (about 70-85%); left dominance is about 10%.
Not B or D: left coronary flow falls in systole, especially to the subendocardium, which is compressed most.
Not E: right coronary flow is not suspended in systole.

questions.stem: The second heart sound is:

options.label: A
options.text: prolonged of low frequency and strong in intensity;

options.label: B
options.text: strong, of low frequence and weak;

options.label: C
options.text: short, of high frequency and weak;

options.label: D
options.text: prolonged of high frequency and strong;

options.label: E
options.text: short, of high frequency and strong in intensity.

questions.explanation:
S2 (closure of aortic and pulmonary valves) is shorter, higher-pitched and usually softer than S1. These semilunar valves are smaller and close sharply against high arterial pressure.
Not A or D: being longer describes S1, which is longer and lower-pitched.
Not B: 'strong' and 'weak' together is self-contradictory.
Not E: S2 is typically softer than S1, especially at the apex.

questions.stem: If on ECG, P wave is missing, but QRS complex and T wave are normal, the pacemaker is located in:
questions.explanation:
Absent P waves with normal QRS and T waves mean the ventricles are activated normally through the His-Purkinje system but the atria are not driving them. This is a junctional (AV nodal) rhythm at about 40-60/min; retrograde P waves may be hidden in the QRS.
Not A: an SA pacemaker produces P waves.
Not C: a His focus is possible but less typical.
Not D or E: Purkinje or ventricular foci produce wide, abnormal QRS complexes.

questions.stem: The isovolumetric contraction is:

options.label: A
options.text: a part of the ejection phase of ventricular contraction;

options.label: B
options.text: a part of the contraction ventricular phase;

options.label: D
options.text: the rapid filling phase of ventricular diastole;

options.label: E
options.text: the slow felling phase of ventricular diastole.

questions.explanation:
Isovolumetric contraction is the first part of ventricular systole (the contraction phase): pressure builds with all valves closed before ejection.
Not A: it comes BEFORE the ejection phase.
Not C: it is systolic, not diastolic.
Not D or E: rapid and slow filling are phases of diastole.

questions.stem: The vascular baroreceptors register change in:
questions.explanation:
Arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch are stretch receptors. They respond to the level of pressure and how quickly it changes, and the reflex mainly defends mean arterial pressure.
Not A or B: systolic and diastolic values affect firing, but the regulated variable is mean pressure.
Not C or E: pCO2 and pO2 are sensed by chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: The asynchronous contraction is:

options.label: A
options.text: a phase of the ventricular systole;

options.label: B
options.text: a phase of the ventricular diastole;

options.label: C
options.text: starts with S - L valves closure;

options.label: D
options.text: ends with S - L valves opening;

questions.explanation:
Asynchronous contraction is the first phase of ventricular systole in the classical phase scheme. Excitation spreads and fibres start contracting at different times, and it ends when the AV valves close and isovolumetric contraction begins.
Not B: it is systolic.
Not C: SL valves close at the start of diastole.
Not D: SL valves open at the end of isovolumetric contraction.
Not E: AV valves open in diastole.

questions.stem: The standard bipolar leads are:
questions.explanation:
Einthoven's standard bipolar limb leads are I (right arm to left arm), II (right arm to left leg) and III (left arm to left leg). Each records the potential difference between two limbs.
Not A: aVR, aVL and aVF are augmented UNIPOLAR limb leads.
Not C: V1-V6 are unipolar precordial (chest) leads.
Not D or E: these combinations include unipolar leads.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not increased during exercise:
questions.explanation:
In exercise, metabolic vasodilation in the large active muscle mass greatly lowers total peripheral resistance, even though vessels constrict in gut, kidney and inactive tissue.
Not A: stroke volume rises (more venous return and contractility).
Not C: systolic pressure rises.
Not D: heart rate rises.
Not E: muscle blood flow rises many-fold.

questions.stem: The peripheral baroreceptors trigger:

options.label: C
options.text: long term regulation of arterial blood pressure;

questions.explanation:
Baroreceptors produce BOTH kinds of reflex. Rising pressure increases their firing, giving a depressor reflex (bradycardia, vasodilation). Falling pressure reduces firing, giving a pressor response (tachycardia, vasoconstriction).
Not B or D: only one direction is wrong.
Not C: baroreceptors reset within days, so they mainly control short-term pressure.
Not E: the Bainbridge reflex comes from atrial volume receptors.

questions.stem: The following would directly increase the heart rate:
questions.explanation:
Sympathetic stimulation acts directly on SA node beta1 receptors, increasing the If and Ca2+ currents and steepening phase 4 depolarisation, which raises heart rate.
Not B: parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation slows the heart.
Not C: low blood pressure raises heart rate only INDIRECTLY, through the baroreceptor reflex.
Not D: it includes B, which is wrong.
Not E: A is correct.

questions.stem: The long term regulation of arterial blood pressure is:

options.label: B
options.text: carried out by pressor and depressor baroreceptive reflexes;

options.label: C
options.text: humoral and restores the volume of blood;

options.label: D
options.text: carried out by depressor chemoreceptive reflexes;

options.label: E
options.text: carried out by ventral medial Hypothalamus.

questions.explanation:
Long-term blood pressure control is humoral and renal, adjusting blood volume through renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, ADH, natriuretic peptides and pressure natriuresis.
Not A or B: nerve and baroreceptor reflexes act in seconds to minutes and reset within days.
Not D: chemoreceptor reflexes mainly respond to blood gases and are not long-term pressure regulators.
Not E: the hypothalamus modulates cardiovascular control but is not the long-term regulator.

questions.stem: The physiological pacemaker of the heart is:
questions.explanation:
The SA node is the physiological pacemaker because its intrinsic firing rate is the fastest, and it suppresses slower pacemakers (overdrive suppression).
Not A: the AV node (40-60/min) takes over only if the SA node fails.
Not B: Purkinje fibres (20-40/min) are tertiary pacemakers.
Not C: the AV bundle (His) is also a subsidiary pacemaker.
Not E: D is correct.

questions.stem: The T wave in ECG indicates:
questions.explanation:
The T wave reflects ventricular repolarisation.
Not A: a resting state gives a flat (isoelectric) baseline, not a wave.
Not B: atrial depolarisation is the P wave.
Not C: SA node activity is too small to appear on the surface ECG.
Not E: Purkinje activation is part of the PR interval and the early QRS.

questions.stem: The end diastolic volume in humans is about:
questions.explanation:
Not scored (reference values vary). Normal adult LV end-diastolic volume is about 120-140 mL, depending on body size and the textbook. The source answer of 140 mL is acceptable, though 120-130 mL is also commonly quoted.
Not B or C: 50-70 mL is close to end-systolic volume or stroke volume.
Not D: 100 mL is low.
Not E: 200 mL suggests a dilated ventricle.
issueNotes: Normal end-diastolic volume varies by size and reference; 140 mL is a plausible representative value in some texts, although typical averages are also quoted near 120–130 mL.

questions.stem: Increased vagal tone causes:
questions.explanation:
Vagal acetylcholine acts on M2 receptors in the SA node, opening K+ channels and reducing the If current. This slows the firing rate (bradycardia).
Not A: vagal activity tends to LOWER blood pressure.
Not B: tachycardia results from vagal withdrawal or sympathetic activity.
Not D: cardiac output falls with a slower rate.
Not E: the vagus has little effect on ventricular force, so stroke volume does not significantly rise.

questions.stem: The diacrotic notch on aortic pressure curve is caused by the:
questions.explanation:
The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure curve marks aortic valve closure. As the ventricle relaxes, blood briefly flows back against the valve; when it shuts, the elastic rebound gives the notch.
Not A or B: AV valve closure happens at the start of systole (S1).
Not D: pulmonary valve closure appears on the pulmonary artery trace, not the aortic one.
Not E: AV valve opening marks the start of filling.

questions.stem: For the peripheral resistance of the blooed flow in a definite region, of highest significance is:

options.label: C
options.text: the laminar blood flow in the vessels;

questions.explanation:
By Poiseuille's law, resistance is proportional to 1/r^4. Small changes in vessel radius (mainly arterioles) therefore change resistance far more than any other factor, which is why arteriolar tone controls regional flow.
Not A: viscosity matters but changes little in health.
Not B: vessel length is essentially fixed.
Not C: laminar flow is a flow pattern, not a determinant of resistance.
Not E: venous valves direct flow but contribute little resistance.

questions.stem: The working myocardium:

options.label: B
options.text: is comprised of cells whose cytoplasm communicates;

options.label: C
options.text: plays the role of pacemaker of the heart;

options.label: D
options.text: is comprised of cells, connected by structures that impede the ion flow;

options.label: E
options.text: reacts to threshold stimuli with different number of excited fibers.

questions.explanation:
Working myocardium is a functional syncytium: cells are separate but electrically coupled by gap junctions, so excitation spreads through the whole chamber and it contracts as one unit.
Not B: the cells keep their own membranes; only ions and small molecules pass through gap junctions, with no continuous cytoplasm.
Not C: pacemaking belongs to specialised conducting tissue.
Not D: the junctions ALLOW ion flow.
Not E: the heart obeys the all-or-none law, so a threshold stimulus excites all fibres.

questions.stem: The heart rate at rest is:
questions.explanation:
In this course a normal adult resting heart rate is about 60-90 beats/min (60-100 in many texts).
Not A: 100-140 is tachycardia.
Not B: 40-60 is bradycardia and the AV junctional rate.
Not C: about 50 is bradycardic (normal only in trained athletes).
Not E: 20-40 is a ventricular (Purkinje) escape rate.

questions.stem: The full compensatory pause is typical of:

options.label: B
options.text: both the atrial and the ventricular extrasystoles;

questions.explanation:
A ventricular extrasystole usually does not conduct back to reset the SA node. The next sinus impulse falls in the ventricles' refractory period and is blocked, and the following one comes on time. So the gap around the premature beat equals two normal cycles: a full compensatory pause.
Not A or B: atrial extrasystoles reset the SA node, giving an incomplete pause.
Not D or E: in atrial fibrillation or flutter there is no regular sinus rhythm to compensate for.

questions.stem: The duration of the cardiac cycle depends on:

options.label: B
options.text: the time needed one systole to occur;

options.label: C
options.text: the time needed one diastole to occur;

questions.explanation:
Cycle duration = 60 / heart rate (e.g. 0.8 s at 75 beats/min). Heart rate therefore determines it, and rising rate mostly shortens diastole.
Not A: stroke volume does not set timing.
Not B, C, E: systole, diastole and pause are PARTS of the cycle; they result from heart rate rather than independently determining it.

questions.stem: The rhythm of the heart is determined by:

options.label: E
options.text: the left and right bundle branches.

questions.explanation:
The sinus (SA) node sets the normal heart rhythm because its spontaneous depolarisation is fastest.
Not A, B, D, E: the His bundle, AV node, Purkinje fibres and bundle branches are slower subsidiary pacemakers and take over only if the SA node fails or conduction is blocked.

questions.stem: The increased heart rate is called:
questions.explanation:
Tachycardia is a heart rate above the normal resting range (above about 90-100 beats/min).
Not A: tachypnoea means rapid BREATHING.
Not B: bradycardia is a SLOW heart rate.
Not C: atrial fibrillation is chaotic atrial activity with an irregular ventricular rate.
Not D: atrial flutter is a specific rapid atrial rhythm. Neither C nor D simply means 'increased heart rate'.

questions.stem: When the rhythm is determined by the AV node, the heart rate is:
questions.explanation:
When the AV node (junction) acts as pacemaker, its intrinsic rate is about 40-60 beats/min.
Not A or C: 60-90 and about 75 are sinus rates.
Not B: 20-40 is a ventricular (Purkinje) escape rate.
Not E: '8-120' is not a physiological pacemaker range.

questions.stem: Automaticity is characteristic for:

options.label: C
options.text: conducting system cells, some neurons and smooth muscle cells;

questions.explanation:
Automaticity (spontaneous generation of impulses) occurs in cardiac conducting system cells, some neurons (e.g. respiratory rhythm generators) and some smooth muscle cells (e.g. gut pacemaker activity, ureter).
Not A: cardiac muscle is not the only automatic tissue, and working myocytes are not automatic.
Not B: skeletal muscle needs nerve stimulation.
Not D: most excitable tissues are not automatic.
Not E: smooth muscle is not the only type.

questions.stem: The action potential of the cardiomyocites is characterized by:

options.label: E
options.text: period of current electrical activity, expressed as slow waves and spike potentials.

questions.explanation:
Ventricular myocyte action potentials have rapid depolarisation (phase 0: fast Na+ influx) followed by slow repolarisation (a long plateau from L-type Ca2+ influx balanced by K+ efflux, then phase 3).
Not A: this suits pacemaker cells only in part, with their slow upstroke.
Not C: rapid depolarisation and repolarisation describes nerve and skeletal muscle.
Not D: depolarisation is fast.
Not E: slow waves with spikes describe gut smooth muscle.

questions.stem: P wave of the electrocardiogram reflects:

options.label: E
options.text: the time necessary for the impulse originating in S.A. node to reach the Purkinje fibers.

questions.explanation:
The P wave reflects atrial depolarisation.
Not A: atrial repolarisation is hidden within the QRS.
Not B: ventricular depolarisation is the QRS.
Not D: hyperpolarisation is not a normal ECG wave.
Not E: the time from SA node to ventricles is the PR interval, not the P wave.

questions.stem: Asynchronous contraction of the ventricles:

options.label: A
options.text: is a phase of the ventricular systole;

options.label: B
options.text: is a phase of the ventricular diastole;

options.label: C
options.text: begins with closing the S.L. valves;

options.label: D
options.text: begins with opening the S.L. valves;

options.label: E
options.text: begins with opening the A.V. valves.

questions.explanation:
Asynchronous contraction is the first phase of ventricular systole in the classical phase scheme. Excitation spreads and fibres start contracting at different times, and it ends when the AV valves close and isovolumetric contraction begins.
Not B: it is systolic.
Not C: SL valves close at the start of diastole.
Not D: SL valves open at the end of isovolumetric contraction.
Not E: AV valves open in diastole.

questions.stem: When there is a complete atriovenrticular block:

options.label: A
options.text: the conductivity at the bundle of His is fully interrupted;

options.label: B
options.text: there is a complete independence of the atrial and ventricular ECG stages;

options.label: C
options.text: the atrial waves indicate normal heart rate, but the rate of ventricular ones is 20-40 bt∙min-1;

options.label: D
options.text: the duration of PQ interval is 0.12-0.20 s;

questions.explanation:
Not scored (source key too broad). The defining feature of complete (third-degree) AV block is total independence of atrial and ventricular activity on the ECG (AV dissociation, B): P waves march at the sinus rate, and QRS complexes come from an escape pacemaker.
Not A: the block can be at the AV node, His bundle or below, not only the His bundle.
Not C: escape rate is about 40-60/min with a junctional escape and 20-40/min with a ventricular escape, so not always 20-40.
Not D: there is no fixed PR interval.
Not E: A and C are not always true.
issueNotes: Complete AV block produces AV dissociation (B). The block can occur at different levels, and ventricular escape rate is not uniformly 20–40 beats/min, so the source key E is not generally valid.

questions.stem: The stroke volume of the heart at rest is:
questions.explanation:
Resting stroke volume is about 70 mL (roughly 60-80 mL): end-diastolic volume (about 120 mL) minus end-systolic volume (about 50 mL).
Not A: beats/min is a unit of heart rate.
Not C: 5.2 L is cardiac output per minute.
Not D: 0.5 L per beat is far too large.
Not E: mmHg is a unit of pressure.

questions.stem: The electrical axis of the heart is determined by:

options.label: A
options.text: the vectorial sum of QRS complexes in the standard leads;

options.label: B
options.text: the vectorial sum of QRS complexes in the precordial leads;

options.label: C
options.text: the vector's direction of the electrical forces of the ventricular muscle tissue;

options.label: D
options.text: the supine or straight position of the body;

options.label: E
options.text: the vector's direction of the electrical forces of the atrial muscle tissue.

questions.explanation:
In practice the electrical axis is found by combining the QRS deflections in the standard limb leads (I, II, III, using Einthoven's triangle) into a single mean vector in the frontal plane.
Not B: precordial leads record the horizontal plane, not the frontal axis. C describes what the axis represents (the mean direction of ventricular depolarisation forces), but the question asks how it is DETERMINED.
Not D: posture can shift the axis slightly but does not determine it.
Not E: atrial forces give the P-wave axis, not the cardiac electrical axis.

questions.stem: The augmented unipolar leads are:

options.label: D
options.text: VI, V2, V3, V4, V5 and V6;

questions.explanation:
The augmented unipolar limb leads are aVR, aVL and aVF. Each compares one limb with the average of the other two, and they are 'augmented' to increase voltage.
Not A: I, II, III are bipolar standard leads.
Not C: it includes the bipolar leads.
Not D: V1-V6 are unipolar chest leads, not augmented limb leads.
Not E: it includes chest leads.

questions.stem: The auscultation of the mitral valve is performed at:

options.label: A
options.text: II-nd sternal intercostal space, right of the sternum;

options.label: B
options.text: V-th intercostal space, 2 cm medial to the midclavicular line;

options.label: C
options.text: IV-th sternal intercostal space, right of the sternum;

options.label: D
options.text: II-nd sternal intercostal space, left of the sternum;

options.label: E
options.text: III-rd sternal intercostal space, left of the sternum.

questions.explanation:
The mitral area is at the apex: the 5th left intercostal space, just medial to the midclavicular line.
Not A: 2nd right intercostal space is the aortic area.
Not C: the tricuspid area is at the lower left sternal border (4th-5th space); the 'right of the sternum' location in this option is not the mitral area.
Not D: 2nd left intercostal space is the pulmonary area.
Not E: 3rd left intercostal space is Erb's point.

questions.stem: The 'plateau'- phase of the cardiomyocytes' action potential is due to:

options.label: A
options.text: outflux of K+ from the cells;

options.label: B
options.text: influx of Na+ into the cells;

options.label: C
options.text: influx of K+ into the cells;

options.label: D
options.text: slow influx of Ca2+ into the cells;

options.label: E
options.text: influx of Na+ into the cells and outlow of K+ from the cells.

questions.explanation:
The plateau (phase 2) is caused by slow Ca2+ influx through L-type channels, balanced against K+ efflux. This keeps the membrane depolarised for about 200 ms and triggers Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release for contraction.
Not A: K+ efflux alone would repolarise the cell (phase 3).
Not B: fast Na+ influx causes the phase 0 upstroke and inactivates quickly.
Not C: K+ normally flows OUT, not in.
Not E: Na+ influx with K+ outflow does not explain the plateau.

questions.stem: The extrasystoles are:

options.label: D
options.text: extraordinary, only currently interrupting the cardiac rhythm, contractions of the cardiac muscle;

questions.explanation:
Extrasystoles are premature beats arising from an ectopic focus, a disturbance of excitability (C). They interrupt the basic rhythm only now and then (D). So E (c and d) is correct.
Not A: rates of 230-250/min describe paroxysmal tachycardia or flutter.
Not B: disturbances of conductivity are heart blocks.

questions.stem: The electrical axis of the heart is of indifferent type when α- angle is:
questions.explanation:
In the classical classification of the electrical axis (alpha angle), the 'indifferent' (intermediate, normal) position is about +30 to +60 degrees.
Not A: +60 to +90 is the vertical position.
Not D: +30 to -30 includes the horizontal position and the start of left deviation.
Not E: beyond -30 is left axis deviation.
Not C: 'from -90 upward' is not a defined normal type.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors is not a vasoconstrictor:
questions.explanation:
Kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) are potent vasodilators that act through endothelial NO and prostacyclin release, and they increase capillary permeability.
Not A: norepinephrine constricts via alpha1.
Not B: epinephrine constricts most beds via alpha1, though it dilates skeletal-muscle vessels via beta2.
Not C: serotonin mainly constricts.
Not D: angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor.

questions.stem: At rest the diastolic arterial pressure is:
questions.explanation:
Not scored (two acceptable answers). Normal resting diastolic pressure lies in the range 60-90 mmHg (C), and 75 mmHg is a typical value within that range (E).
Not A: 90-95 mmHg is hypertensive.
Not B and D: 100-160 mmHg are systolic values, or a hypertensive crisis if diastolic.
issueNotes: Both the typical range 60–90 mmHg (C) and the particular example 75 mmHg (E) may describe normal resting diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following doesn't affect the gradient of the blood pressure:
questions.explanation:
The pressure gradient in the circulation is set by cardiac output and total peripheral resistance (P = Q x R), and resistance depends on blood viscosity. Blood volume affects filling and therefore output and pressure. Minute respiratory volume (ventilation) is a respiratory variable and has no direct effect, so B is correct.
Not A, C, D, E: each directly affects pressure.

questions.stem: Throughout the isovolumetrtc relaxation of the ventricles:

options.label: A
options.text: A.V. valves are opened, S.L. valves - opened;

options.label: B
options.text: A.V. valves are closed, S.L. valves - opened;

options.label: C
options.text: A.V. valves are opened, S.L. valves - closed;

options.label: D
options.text: A.V. valves are closed, S.L. valves - closed;

questions.explanation:
In isovolumetric relaxation, ventricular pressure has fallen below arterial pressure (SL valves closed) but is still above atrial pressure (AV valves closed). With all valves closed, pressure falls but volume stays constant.
Not A: both are never open together.
Not B: SL valves are open during ejection.
Not C: this describes ventricular filling.
Not E: D is correct.

questions.stem: The first heart sound is:

options.label: A
options.text: systolic, result of the ventricular contractions;

options.label: B
options.text: systolic, result of'the A.V. valves closing;

options.label: C
options.text: systolic, result of the S.L valves closing;

options.label: D
options.text: diastolic, result of the A.V. valves closing;

questions.explanation:
S1 marks the start of ventricular systole. It is caused mainly by closure of the AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves as the contracting ventricles raise pressure above atrial pressure, together with vibration of the tensed ventricular walls and blood. So A and B together (E) is correct.
Not C: SL valve closure produces S2.
Not D: S1 is systolic, not diastolic.

questions.stem: Cardiac output (C.O.) depends on:
questions.explanation:
Cardiac output = stroke volume x heart rate (B, C), and stroke volume depends on preload, afterload and contractility (D). So E is correct.
Not A: vital capacity is a lung volume and has no direct link to cardiac output.

questions.stem: The intracardial regulation of the heart is carried out by:

options.label: D
options.text: adaptation to changes in venous return or the change in peripheral resistance;

questions.explanation:
Intracardiac (intrinsic) regulation is the heart's self-adjustment without nerves or hormones. It adapts to venous return through the heterometric Frank-Starling mechanism and to changes in peripheral resistance through homeometric mechanisms such as the Anrep effect.
Not A, B, C: reflex, neural and humoral regulation are EXTRACARDIAC.
Not E: automaticity generates the rhythm but does not adapt output to load.

questions.stem: The heart would stop in diastole because of:

options.label: A
options.text: increased level of Ca2+ in the extracellular fluid;

options.label: D
options.text: increased concentration of K+ in the extracellular fluid (above 8 mmol.l-1);

options.label: E
options.text: increased secretion of T3 and T4.

questions.explanation:
High extracellular K+ (above about 8 mmol/L) depolarises the resting membrane and inactivates fast Na+ channels. Excitability and conduction fail and the heart stops in a relaxed (diastolic) state; this is the principle of cardioplegia solutions.
Not A: high Ca2+ tends to cause arrest in contraction (systole).
Not B, C, E: catecholamines, glucocorticoids and thyroid hormones increase rate and/or contractility.

questions.stem: When the heart rate is 60 bt∙min-1, the duration of the cardiac cycle is:
questions.explanation:
Cycle duration = 60 / heart rate = 60 / 60 = 1 s.
Not A: 0.5 s corresponds to 120 beats/min.
Not B: 0.8 s corresponds to 75 beats/min.
Not D: 0.2 s would mean 300 beats/min.
Not E: C is correct.

questions.stem: The pulse pressure is:

options.label: A
options.text: closer in value to the systolic than to the diastolic pressure;

options.label: B
options.text: mean arithmetic of systolic and diastolic pressures;

options.label: C
options.text: closer in value to the diastolic than to the systolic pressure;

options.label: D
options.text: the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressure;

options.label: E
options.text: one third of the mean arterial pressure.

questions.explanation:
Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure (e.g. 120 - 80 = 40 mmHg). It reflects mainly stroke volume and arterial compliance.
Not A or C: it is a difference, not a value near either pressure.
Not B: the simple average of systolic and diastolic is not a standard measure; MAP is about diastolic + one third of pulse pressure.
Not E: one third of pulse pressure (not of MAP) is added to diastolic pressure to estimate MAP.

questions.stem: The cardiovascular center is situated in:
questions.explanation:
The cardiovascular (vasomotor and cardioinhibitory) centre is in the medulla oblongata, including the nucleus tractus solitarius, rostral ventrolateral medulla and nucleus ambiguus/dorsal vagal nucleus.
Not A or C: the hypothalamus and cortex influence it but are higher centres.
Not B: the midbrain is not the main centre.
Not E: T1-L2 spinal segments contain the sympathetic preganglionic neurons it controls.

questions.stem: In the pulmonary circulation blood leaves the:

options.label: A
options.text: right ventricle and goes directly to the aorta;

options.label: B
options.text: right ventricle and moves to the lungs;

options.label: C
options.text: right atrium and goes directly to the left ventricle;

options.label: D
options.text: right atrium and goes directly to the lungs;

options.label: E
options.text: left ventricle and moves to the lungs.

questions.explanation:
In the pulmonary circulation, deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and arteries to the lungs.
Not A: the aorta receives blood from the LEFT ventricle.
Not C: the right atrium empties into the RIGHT ventricle.
Not D: the right atrium does not connect directly to the lungs.
Not E: the left ventricle supplies the systemic circulation.

questions.stem: In the systemic circulation, blood leaves the:

options.label: A
options.text: left ventricle and goes directly to the aorta;

options.label: B
options.text: right ventricle and goes directly to the aorta;

options.label: C
options.text: right ventricle and moves to the lungs;

options.label: D
options.text: lungs and moves to the left atrium;

options.label: E
options.text: right atrium and goes directly to the lungs.

questions.explanation:
In the systemic circulation, oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve into the aorta.
Not B: the right ventricle supplies the pulmonary trunk.
Not C: that is the pulmonary circulation.
Not D: lungs to left atrium is the END of the pulmonary circulation.
Not E: the right atrium does not send blood directly to the lungs.

questions.stem: The cardiac cycle includes all of the following events except:

options.label: A
options.text: the movement of impulses from the SA node to all regions of the heart wall;

options.label: B
options.text: the closing and opening of the heart valves during each heart beat;

options.label: C
options.text: the number of times the heart beats in one minute;

options.label: D
options.text: the changes in pressure gradients in all chambers of the heart;

options.label: E
options.text: the changes in blood volume in all chambers of the heart.

questions.explanation: Heart rate is the NUMBER of cycles per minute, a rate rather than an event within a single cycle, so C is the exception. A single cardiac cycle includes the spread of excitation from the SA node (A), valve opening and closing (B), and pressure (D) and volume (E) changes in every chamber.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances does not participate in the regulation of blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
As worded, 'nitric acid' (HNO3) is a strong mineral acid with no physiological role in blood-pressure regulation, so D is the intended answer. Be careful: if NITRIC OXIDE was meant, it is a key endothelial vasodilator that does regulate pressure.
Not A: ADH (vasopressin) constricts vessels and retains water.
Not B: ANP causes vasodilation and natriuresis.
Not C: angiotensin II constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone.
Not E: epinephrine raises cardiac output and affects vascular tone.

questions.stem: Exchange of nutrients and gases between the blood and tissue cells is the main function of the:
questions.explanation:
Capillaries are the exchange vessels. They have walls one endothelial cell thick, an enormous total surface area and slow flow, which allows diffusion of gases, nutrients and wastes.
Not A: arterioles are resistance vessels.
Not B: arteries are conducting and pressure-reservoir vessels.
Not C: veins are capacitance (blood-reservoir) vessels.
Not E: venules allow some exchange and leukocyte migration but are not the main exchange site.

questions.stem: In the heart, (within physiological limits) the strength of contraction is directly proportional to the:

options.label: C
options.text: initial length of the cardiac muscle;

questions.explanation:
The Frank-Starling law: within physiological limits, force of contraction increases with the initial (end-diastolic) length of the muscle fibres. More stretch improves actin-myosin overlap and troponin's Ca2+ sensitivity.
Not A: pacemaker activity sets rate.
Not B: the AV nodal delay is a timing feature.
Not D: respiratory rate is unrelated.
Not E: the ST segment is an ECG feature, not a cause of force.

questions.stem: The inferior vena cava brings blood from the lower regions of the body and empties into the:
questions.explanation:
The inferior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the lower body to the right atrium, as does the superior vena cava from the upper body.
Not A: the left atrium receives the pulmonary veins.
Not C: the aorta carries blood away from the left ventricle.
Not D or E: the veins drain into the atria, not directly into the ventricles.

questions.stem: The pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.explanation:
The SA node is the normal pacemaker because it has the fastest spontaneous depolarisation rate (about 60-100/min).
Not A: Purkinje fibres are the slowest (20-40/min).
Not B or C: bundle branches and His bundle are subsidiary pacemakers.
Not D: the AV node is the secondary pacemaker (40-60/min).

questions.stem: The tricuspid valve is located between the:
questions.explanation:
The tricuspid valve, with three cusps, lies between the right atrium and right ventricle.
Not A or B: the septa, not valves, separate the two atria and the two ventricles.
Not D: the mitral (bicuspid) valve is between the left atrium and ventricle.
Not E: the right ventricle opens into the pulmonary trunk through the pulmonary valve; the aorta is guarded by the aortic valve on the left.

questions.stem: When the mitral valve closes, it prevents the backflow of blood from the:

options.label: A
options.text: left atrium into the left ventricle;

options.label: B
options.text: left ventricle into the left atrium;

options.label: C
options.text: right atrium into the right ventricle;

options.label: E
options.text: right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.

questions.explanation:
During ventricular systole, LV pressure exceeds left atrial pressure; the closed mitral valve stops blood flowing back from the LV into the LA. Regurgitation through this valve produces an apical systolic murmur.
Not A: in diastole, flow from LA to LV is forward.
Not C: this concerns the tricuspid valve.
Not D: flow from LV to aorta is normal ejection, not backflow.
Not E: this concerns the pulmonary valve.

questions.stem: Which of the following elements of the conducting system has the slowest velocity of conduction:
questions.explanation:
The AV node conducts slowest (about 0.02-0.05 m/s), giving the AV delay that lets the atria finish filling the ventricles.
Not A: the SA node also conducts slowly, but the AV node is the classic slowest point.
Not B: atrial muscle conducts at about 0.3-1 m/s.
Not C: Purkinje fibres are the fastest (about 2-4 m/s).
Not E: the His bundle conducts at about 1-2 m/s.

questions.stem: The myocardium functions as a functional syncytium due to:

options.label: A
options.text: the presence of striations in the myocardium;

options.label: C
options.text: the presence of gap junctions (intercalated disks);

questions.explanation:
The intercalated discs between myocytes contain gap junctions (connexin channels) that let ions flow directly from cell to cell, so excitation spreads as if through one cell. This makes the heart a functional syncytium.
Not A: striations reflect sarcomere organisation.
Not B: branching helps form a network but does not couple cells electrically.
Not D: desmosomes provide MECHANICAL attachment.
Not E: Ca2+ affects contraction strength, not electrical coupling.

questions.stem: Positive bathmotropic effect on the heart is produced by:
questions.explanation:
Bathmotropy means excitability. Sympathetic stimulation (noradrenaline at beta1 receptors) increases excitability, a positive bathmotropic effect, along with positive chrono-, ino- and dromotropic effects.
Not A: vagal stimulation is negatively bathmotropic.
Not C or D: atropine and vagotomy only REMOVE vagal inhibition rather than directly stimulating the heart.
Not E: raised K+ depolarises cells and inactivates Na+ channels, reducing excitability.

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricle increases during:

options.label: D
options.text: stimulation of parasympathetic nerves to the heart;

questions.explanation:
Myocardial hypoxia releases vasodilator metabolites (adenosine, K+, H+, CO2, NO), which dilate coronary arterioles and increase flow; metabolic control dominates coronary regulation.
Not A: early systole compresses intramural LV vessels, so flow is LOWEST then.
Not C: hypothermia lowers metabolic demand and flow.
Not D: vagal stimulation slows the heart, lowering demand, so flow does not rise significantly.
Not E: AV block slows the ventricular rate and reduces demand.

questions.stem: Local metabolic activity is the main factor determining the rate of blood flow to the:
questions.explanation:
Coronary blood flow is set mainly by local metabolic activity: myocardial O2 demand produces adenosine and other vasodilators, because the heart already extracts most of the O2 delivered and can only meet demand by raising flow.
Not B: skin flow is controlled mainly by sympathetic nerves for thermoregulation.
Not C: gland flow is largely neurally linked to secretion.
Not D: lung flow is passive and shaped by hypoxic vasoconstriction.
Not E: renal flow is autoregulated (myogenic, tubuloglomerular feedback) to stabilise filtration, not matched to metabolism.

questions.stem: Blood brain barrier is made up of:
questions.explanation:
Not scored (incomplete options). The blood-brain barrier is formed mainly by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells, supported by the basement membrane, pericytes and astrocyte end-feet. Endothelial cells are not among the options, so A (astrocytes, which induce and maintain the barrier) is the closest listed component.
Not B or C: oligodendrocytes (oligodendroglia) form CNS myelin.
Not D: microglia are immune cells.
issueNotes: Astrocyte end-feet (A) support the BBB, but its restrictive barrier is formed primarily by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells, which are absent from the choices. A is only the closest listed constituent.

questions.stem: The second heart sound differs from the first heart sound in that it is:

options.label: A
options.text: related to turbulence set up by valve closure;

options.label: B
options.text: longer lasting than the first sound;

options.label: E
options.text: heard when the ventricles are contracting.

questions.explanation:
Not scored (more than one correct answer). Compared with S1, S2 is higher in frequency (C), because small semilunar valves close against high arterial pressure. S2 is also physiologically split, especially in inspiration when pulmonary closure is delayed (D).
Not A: both sounds relate to valve closure, so this is no difference.
Not B: S2 is SHORTER than S1.
Not E: S2 is heard at the START of ventricular relaxation (diastole).
issueNotes: S2 is higher pitched than S1 (C) and can physiologically split, especially during inspiration (D). Multiple options are correct.

questions.stem: Pulmonary vascular resistance is:

options.label: A
options.text: is equal to that offered by the systemic circuit;

options.label: B
options.text: decreased when alveolar oxygen pressure falls;

options.label: C
options.text: expressed in units of volume flow per unit time per unit pressure gradient;

options.label: E
options.text: regulated reflexvely by sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves.

questions.explanation:
During exercise, the higher cardiac output recruits previously closed pulmonary capillaries and distends open ones, so pulmonary vascular resistance FALLS and pulmonary pressure rises only slightly.
Not A: PVR is about one-tenth of systemic resistance.
Not B: low alveolar O2 causes hypoxic vasoconstriction, which INCREASES resistance.
Not C: resistance is pressure difference divided by flow (e.g. mmHg per L/min).
Not E: sympathetic control of pulmonary vessels is weak, and the circulation is mostly passively regulated.

questions.stem: Which of vessels mentioned below are not under sympathetic control:
questions.explanation:
Not scored (overstated wording). Cerebral vessels are the intended answer because their flow is controlled mainly by local metabolic (especially CO2) and myogenic autoregulation, with little effect from sympathetic nerves. They do have sympathetic innervation, though, so 'not under sympathetic control' is too strong.
Not B, D, E: splanchnic, cutaneous and skeletal-muscle vessels are strongly controlled by sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerves.
Not C: coronary vessels have sympathetic innervation, though metabolic control dominates.
issueNotes: Cerebral vessels do receive sympathetic innervation, though local metabolic/myogenic mechanisms predominate. A is the intended relative answer, but "not under sympathetic control" is literally too strong.

questions.stem: In the heart:

options.label: A
options.text: the left atrial wall is about three times thicker than the right atrial wall;

options.label: B
options.text: systolic contraction normally begins in the left atrium;

options.label: C
options.text: excitation spreads directly from atrial muscle cells to ventricular muscle cells;

options.label: D
options.text: atrial and ventricular muscle contracts simultaneously in systole;

options.label: E
options.text: the contracting ventricles shorten from apex to base.

questions.explanation:
As the ventricles contract, the base (AV valve plane) is pulled down towards the fairly fixed apex, shortening the ventricle along its long axis.
Not A: the threefold wall difference applies to the VENTRICLES (LV vs RV); the atrial walls are similar.
Not B: excitation starts at the SA node in the RIGHT atrium.
Not C: the fibrous skeleton blocks direct atrial-ventricular muscle conduction, so the only route is through the AV node and His bundle.
Not D: atrial systole comes before ventricular systole.

questions.stem: When measuring blood pressure by the auscultatory method:

options.label: A
options.text: the sounds that are heard are generated in the heart;

options.label: B
options.text: the cuff pressure at which the first sounds are heard indicate the systolic pressure;

options.label: C
options.text: the cuff pressure at which the loudest sounds are heard indicate diastolic pressure;

options.label: D
options.text: systolic pressure estimations tend to be lower than those made by the palpatory method;

options.label: E
options.text: wider cuffs are required for smaller arms.

questions.explanation:
As the cuff deflates, the first tapping Korotkoff sounds (phase I) mark the systolic pressure: blood begins to spurt through the partly compressed artery.
Not A: the sounds come from turbulence in the brachial artery, not the heart.
Not C: diastolic pressure is taken at disappearance (phase V) or muffling (phase IV), not at the loudest sounds.
Not D: palpatory readings tend to be LOWER, so auscultatory systolic is higher.
Not E: LARGER arms need wider cuffs; a cuff too small overestimates pressure.

questions.stem: The absolute refractory period in the ventricles:

options.label: A
options.text: is the period when the ventricles are completely still excitable;

options.label: B
options.text: corresponds to the period of ventricular depolarization;

options.label: C
options.text: corresponds approximately to the period of ventricular relaxation;

options.label: D
options.text: is shorter than the corresponding period in atrial muscle;

options.label: E
options.text: decreases during parasympathetic stimulation of the heart.

questions.explanation:
Not scored (approximate wording). The ventricular absolute refractory period runs from the upstroke through the plateau to about mid-repolarisation (about 200-250 ms), during which no stimulus can trigger another action potential. B is the intended answer, describing it roughly as ventricular depolarisation.
Not A: the cells are INEXCITABLE in this period.
Not C: it coincides mostly with contraction, not relaxation.
Not D: ventricular refractory periods are LONGER than atrial.
Not E: vagal stimulation shortens ATRIAL refractoriness and has little effect on ventricles.
issueNotes: The ventricular absolute refractory period extends through depolarisation, the plateau, and part of repolarisation; B is a rough rather than exact description.

questions.stem: When the eye balls are pressed the reflex that is triggered is called:
questions.explanation:
Pressing on the eyeballs triggers the oculocardiac (Aschner-Dagnini) reflex. The ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve carries the signal to the vagal nuclei, causing bradycardia.
Not A: the Goltz reflex is bradycardia or arrest from a blow or tapping on the abdomen.
Not B: a pressor reflex raises pressure.
Not C: the Bezold-Jarisch reflex comes from ventricular receptors (bradycardia, hypotension).
Not E: 'depressor reflex' is a general term; the specific named reflex is D.

questions.stem: When the heart rate is 75 bt∙min-1, the duration of the cardiac cycle is:
questions.explanation:
Cycle duration = 60 / heart rate = 60 / 75 = 0.8 s (about 0.3 s systole and 0.5 s diastole).
Not A: 1 s corresponds to 60 beats/min.
Not B: 0.6 s corresponds to 100 beats/min.
Not C: 1.2 s corresponds to 50 beats/min.
Not E: 1.5 s corresponds to 40 beats/min.

questions.stem: Hyperaemia in skeletal muscle during exercise is normally associated with:

options.label: A
options.text: release of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone in the exercising muscles;

options.label: B
options.text: capillary dilation due to relaxation of capillary smooth muscle;

options.label: D
options.text: reflex vasoconstriction in other vascular beds;

questions.explanation:
During exercise, sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood from splanchnic, renal and inactive tissues, which helps send cardiac output to the dilated active muscles.
Not A: sympathetic outflow to exercising muscle actually rises, but local metabolites override it (functional sympatholysis).
Not B: capillaries have no smooth muscle; arterioles and precapillary sphincters relax.
Not C: arterial pressure rises.
Not E: the muscle pump and venous valves keep venous pressure in exercising limbs low.

questions.stem: Sinoatrial node cells are:

options.label: C
options.text: unable to generate impulses when completely denervated;

options.label: D
options.text: connected to the AV node by fine bundles of Purkinje tissue;

options.label: E
options.text: able to self generate impulses because their membrane potential is unstable.

questions.explanation:
SA node cells have an unstable resting potential: in phase 4 they slowly depolarise (funny current If, then T-type and L-type Ca2+ currents) until they reach threshold. This lets them generate impulses on their own.
Not A: the SA node is only in the RIGHT atrium.
Not B: it is innervated by AUTONOMIC (vagal and sympathetic) nerves, not somatic nerves.
Not C: a denervated SA node still fires (e.g. transplanted hearts).
Not D: SA-to-AV conduction is through atrial muscle and internodal pathways, not Purkinje bundles.

questions.stem: The first heart sound corresponds in time with:

options.label: A
options.text: closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves;

options.label: B
options.text: the P wave of the electrocardiogram;

options.label: E
options.text: the A wave in central venous pressure.

questions.explanation:
S1 happens at the start of ventricular systole, when rising ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and the AV valves close.
Not A: semilunar valve closure is S2.
Not B: the P wave (atrial depolarisation) comes BEFORE S1.
Not C: atrial pressure rises slightly (c wave) as the closed AV valves bulge back.
Not E: the A wave is atrial contraction, which comes before S1.

questions.stem: Absolute refractory period in the heart:

options.label: A
options.text: corresponds to the duration of relaxation;

options.label: B
options.text: lasts till half of cardiac contraction;

options.label: C
options.text: shorter than refractory period in skeletal muscle;

questions.explanation:
Not scored (approximate wording). The cardiac absolute refractory period is long (about 0.25 s) and lasts through most of mechanical contraction, so the heart cannot be re-excited until it starts to relax and cannot be tetanised. D is the intended answer, though the refractory period does not end exactly when contraction ends.
Not A: it does not cover relaxation.
Not B: it lasts beyond the first half of contraction.
Not C: it is LONGER than in skeletal muscle (about 1-2 ms).
Not E: 10 ms is far too short.
issueNotes: The long absolute refractory period overlaps most of cardiac contraction, but its end is not exactly aligned with completion of mechanical contraction.

questions.stem: The strength of contraction of left ventricular muscle increases when:
questions.explanation:
Higher end-diastolic filling pressure means greater end-diastolic volume and fibre stretch, so contraction is stronger (Frank-Starling).
Not B: high K+ depolarises cells and weakens contraction, and can cause diastolic arrest.
Not C: low Ca2+ reduces contractile force.
Not D: low Mg2+ mainly causes arrhythmias.
Not E: lower afterload lets the ventricle shorten more and eject more, but it does not increase the force developed by the muscle.

questions.stem: When parasympaticus is activated, there is:
questions.explanation:
Parasympathetic (vagal) activation releases acetylcholine on M2 receptors in the SA node, slowing the heart (bradycardia) and AV conduction.
Not A: it tends to lower, not raise, blood pressure.
Not B: tachycardia results from sympathetic activity or vagal withdrawal.
Not D: vagal supply to the ventricles is sparse, so stroke volume does not rise.
Not E: C is correct.

questions.stem: Cardiac output:

options.label: A
options.text: is normally expressed as the output of each of the ventricles in litre/minute-1;

options.label: E
options.text: does not increase in exercise following denervation of the heart.

questions.explanation:
Cardiac output is defined as the volume pumped by EACH ventricle per minute, expressed in L/min (about 5 L/min at rest).
Not B: 2.0 L/min is far too low for a resting adult.
Not C: 10 L/min occurs only with moderate exertion.
Not D: cold causes skin vasoconstriction and has no major effect on output (shivering may raise it slightly).
Not E: a denervated heart still raises output in exercise, through circulating catecholamines and the Frank-Starling mechanism.

questions.stem: In the brachial artery:

options.label: A
options.text: pulse waves travel at the same velocity as blood;

options.label: B
options.text: pulse pressure falls with decreasing elasticity of the wall;

options.label: C
options.text: pressure rises markedly when the artery is occluded distally;

options.label: D
options.text: pressure falls when the arm is raised above head level;

options.label: E
options.text: pulse pressures have a smaller amplitude than aortic pulse pressures.

questions.explanation:
Raising the arm above heart level adds a negative hydrostatic column (about 0.77 mmHg per cm above the heart), so brachial pressure falls.
Not A: the pulse wave travels at about 4-10 m/s, far faster than blood itself (about 0.2-0.5 m/s).
Not B: stiffer walls INCREASE pulse pressure.
Not C: distal occlusion raises pressure only slightly, not markedly.
Not E: peripheral wave reflection usually makes brachial pulse pressure LARGER than aortic.

questions.stem: From functional point of view arterioles:

options.label: A
options.text: allow exchange of water, salts, electrolytes, hormones and other substances between plasma and tissues in both directions;

options.label: B
options.text: contain bigger part of the blood volume;

options.label: C
options.text: decrease the big fluctuations in blood plasma during the cardiac cycle;

options.label: D
options.text: form the resistance against the ventricular contractions;

options.label: E
options.text: play the role of reservoirs of blood from the capillaries.

questions.explanation:
Arterioles are the main resistance vessels. Their smooth-muscle tone creates the largest pressure drop in the circulation, sets total peripheral resistance (the afterload against which the ventricles eject) and controls flow into capillary beds.
Not A: exchange is a capillary function.
Not B: veins hold most of the blood.
Not C: smoothing of pressure fluctuations is mainly done by the elastic arteries (Windkessel effect).
Not E: veins are the blood reservoirs.

questions.stem: In a denervated heart, the left ventricular stroke volume increases when the:

options.label: A
options.text: end-diastolic length of the ventricular fibres increases;

questions.explanation:
Without nerves, the heart still adjusts stroke volume intrinsically. Greater end-diastolic fibre length gives a stronger contraction (Frank-Starling), so stroke volume rises.
Not B: lower resistance can raise stroke volume briefly, but stroke volume cannot stay above venous return; A is the main intrinsic mechanism.
Not C: falling blood volume reduces filling and stroke volume.
Not D: lower RV output reduces LV filling.
Not E: venodilation pools blood and reduces venous return.

questions.stem: The greater the distance from the heart, the arterial:

options.label: A
options.text: walls contain relatively more smooth muscle fibers than elastic;

options.label: B
options.text: flow has a greater tendency to be turbulent;

options.label: C
options.text: mean pressure tends to decrease slightly;

options.label: D
options.text: pulse pressure tends to increase slightly;

questions.explanation:
Not scored (no source key, several defensible answers). Moving away from the heart, artery walls become relatively more muscular and less elastic (A). Mean pressure falls only slightly through large and medium arteries (C). Wave reflection amplifies systolic and pulse pressure peripherally (D).
Not B: smaller vessels and lower velocities make turbulence LESS likely.
Not E: arterial pO2 stays essentially unchanged until blood reaches the capillaries.
issueNotes: This item has no source answer printed. Distal arteries have relatively more smooth muscle (A); mean pressure generally falls with distance (C); peripheral systolic/pulse-pressure amplification can make D true. A, C and D are defensible.

questions.stem: The heart rate is decreased when:
questions.explanation:
Vagal stimulation releases acetylcholine at the SA node, slowing its firing and so decreasing heart rate.
Not A: atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and INCREASES heart rate.
Not C: glucocorticoids enhance catecholamine effects and do not slow the heart.
Not D: Ca2+ mainly increases contractility.
Not E: adrenaline increases heart rate through beta1 receptors.

questions.stem: Systemic hypertension may be caused by:

options.label: A
options.text: hypoxia due to chronic respiratory failure;

options.label: D
options.text: myocardial thickening (hypertrophy) of the left ventricle;

options.label: E
options.text: the rapid cardiac action of ventricular fibrillation.

questions.explanation:
Excess aldosterone (e.g. primary hyperaldosteronism, Conn's syndrome) causes renal Na+ and water retention and expands blood volume, producing systemic hypertension (often with hypokalaemia).
Not A: chronic hypoxia causes PULMONARY hypertension through hypoxic vasoconstriction.
Not C: excess insulin is not a classic direct cause.
Not D: LV hypertrophy is a CONSEQUENCE of hypertension, not a cause.
Not E: ventricular fibrillation produces no effective output and pressure collapses.

questions.stem: The main factor, determining the diastolic blood pressure is:

options.label: E
options.text: the length of the blood vessel.

questions.explanation:
Diastolic pressure depends mainly on how quickly blood runs off from the arteries during diastole, which is set by peripheral (arteriolar) resistance; heart rate also contributes by changing the length of diastole.
Not A: blood volume influences all pressures through cardiac output but is not the main determinant of diastolic pressure.
Not B: viscosity changes little normally.
Not C: cardiac performance (stroke volume) mainly affects SYSTOLIC and pulse pressure.
Not E: vessel length is essentially constant.

questions.stem: In atrial fibrillation:

options.label: A
options.text: the electrocardiogram shows no evidence of atrial activity;

options.label: B
options.text: the ventricular rate is lower than atrial rate;

options.label: C
options.text: respiratory sinus arrhythmia can usually be registered;

options.label: D
options.text: the ventricular rate is higher than atrial rate;

options.label: E
options.text: the QRS complex has abnormal configuration.

questions.explanation:
In AF the atria fire chaotically at about 350-600/min, but the AV node's refractoriness lets only some impulses through. The ventricular rate is therefore much lower and irregularly irregular.
Not A: the ECG shows fibrillatory (f) waves, not true P waves, so there is still evidence of atrial activity.
Not C: respiratory sinus arrhythmia needs sinus rhythm.
Not D: the ventricular rate cannot exceed the atrial rate.
Not E: QRS complexes are usually narrow and normal unless there is bundle branch block.

questions.stem: Fenestrated capillaries:

options.label: B
options.text: are located in most of the tissues;

options.label: C
options.text: permit only one-way exchange of materials;

options.label: D
options.text: have a layer of smooth muscle in their walls;

options.label: E
options.text: are found in the liver and kidneys.

questions.explanation:
Fenestrated capillaries have pores (fenestrae, about 60-80 nm) in their endothelial cells, allowing rapid exchange. They are found in renal glomeruli, endocrine glands, the intestinal mucosa and choroid plexus.
Not B: most tissues (muscle, skin, lung) have continuous capillaries.
Not C: exchange goes in both directions.
Not D: capillaries have no smooth muscle.
Not E: the kidney has fenestrated capillaries, but the liver has discontinuous sinusoids, so E is only partly true.

questions.stem: The mean arterial blood pressure is about:

options.label: A
options.text: close in value to systolic, rather than the diastolic;

options.label: B
options.text: the average of systolic and diastolic blood pressure;

options.label: C
options.text: the diastolic plus one third of the pulse pressure

options.label: D
options.text: the difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures;

options.label: E
options.text: the systolic plus one third of the diastolic pressure.

questions.explanation:
MAP is about diastolic + one third of pulse pressure (e.g. 80 + 40/3 = about 93 mmHg). This is because the heart spends about two thirds of each cycle in diastole at rest.
Not A: MAP is closer to DIASTOLIC pressure.
Not B: the simple average overestimates MAP at normal heart rates.
Not D: systolic minus diastolic is pulse pressure.
Not E: the formula is wrong (it would exceed systolic).

questions.stem: The cardiac output (C.O.):

options.label: A
options.text: the volume of blood, pumped by the right ventricle per minute;

options.label: B
options.text: the volume of blood, flowing through the systemic circulation per minute;

options.label: C
options.text: is a function of stroke volume and heart rate;

options.label: D
options.text: the volume of blood ejected by the right ventricle;

options.label: E
options.text: the volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle.

questions.explanation:
Not scored (more than one correct answer). In a steady state the outputs of both ventricles and the systemic flow are equal, so A (RV output per minute) and B (systemic flow per minute) are both correct. C (a function of stroke volume and heart rate: CO = SV x HR) is also correct.
Not D and E: these give the volume per BEAT (stroke volume) without the 'per minute' element.
issueNotes: A and B both describe flow per minute in the steady circulation, while C gives cardiac output as stroke volume × heart rate. All three are correct. questions.stem: The velocity of arterial pulse coduction:

options.label: A
options.text: depends on the blood flow velocity;

options.label: B
options.text: is equal for the big and small ateries;

options.label: C
options.text: depends on the arterial wall peculiarities;

options.label: E
options.text: in lower in the smaller arteries.

questions.explanation:
Pulse wave velocity depends on the properties of the arterial wall: stiffness (elastic modulus), wall thickness and lumen radius (Moens-Korteweg equation). Stiffer walls transmit the wave faster.
Not A: the wave travels far faster than blood and is independent of blood velocity.
Not B: velocity is higher in smaller, stiffer peripheral arteries.
Not D: arteries stiffen with age, so pulse wave velocity increases.
Not E: it is HIGHER, not lower, in smaller arteries.

questions.stem: Hardening of the arterial walls tends to raise:
questions.explanation:
Stiff arterial walls reduce compliance, so the same stroke volume produces a higher systolic peak. Diastolic pressure tends to fall because there is less elastic recoil, and pulse pressure widens (isolated systolic hypertension of the elderly).
Not A: compliance DECREASES.
Not C: diastolic pressure tends to fall or stay the same.
Not D: peripheral resistance is set by arterioles, not large-artery stiffness.
Not E: breathing frequency is unrelated.

questions.stem: Left ventricular failure tends to cause an increase in:

options.label: E
options.text: pulmonary oedema when the patient stands up.

questions.explanation:
In LV failure the ventricle cannot empty properly, so pressure backs up into the left atrium and pulmonary veins. This raises pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, causing congestion and pulmonary oedema.
Not A: right atrial pressure rises only later, if right heart failure follows.
Not B: ejection fraction usually FALLS.
Not D: lung compliance falls as the lungs become congested.
Not E: oedema and breathlessness worsen when LYING down (orthopnoea) and improve when sitting or standing.

questions.stem: Which of following factors doesn`t play role in the formation of the Effective Filtration Pressure in the capillaries:

options.label: B
options.text: the coloid osmotic pressure of plasma protein;

questions.explanation: Effective filtration pressure is set by the Starling forces: capillary hydrostatic (haemodynamic) pressure (A), plasma colloid osmotic pressure (B), tissue fluid hydrostatic pressure (D) and interstitial colloid osmotic pressure (E). Intrapleural pressure (C) acts within the thorax for lung mechanics and is not a Starling force in systemic capillaries.

questions.stem: If the vagus nerve innervating the heart is blocked, than:

options.label: E
options.text: the heart activity would remain unchanged.

questions.explanation:
At rest, vagal tone holds the heart well below the SA node's intrinsic rate (about 100/min). Blocking the vagus (e.g. atropine or vagotomy) removes this brake and heart rate increases.
Not A: rate rises, not falls.
Not B or C: stroke volume may fall slightly with shorter filling time, but cardiac output usually stays the same or rises.
Not E: activity changes because vagal tone is normally present.

questions.stem: The plateau phase of the action potential of the contractile myocardiocytes is due to:

options.label: A
options.text: the slow movement of Na+ across the cell membrane;

options.label: C
options.text: the increased membrane permeability to K+;

options.label: D
options.text: the increased membrane permeability to Na+;

options.label: E
options.text: a decrease in Ca2+ diffusing across membrane.

questions.explanation:
The plateau (phase 2) of contractile myocyte action potentials comes from Ca2+ influx through L-type (slow) Ca2+ channels, balanced by K+ efflux. This Ca2+ also triggers SR Ca2+ release for contraction.
Not A or D: Na+ entry causes the rapid upstroke (phase 0), and the fast Na+ channels then inactivate.
Not C: a large rise in K+ permeability causes repolarisation (phase 3).
Not E: a DECREASE in Ca2+ entry would shorten the plateau.
